claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by the kinetic balance between mechanical passive-film removal and chemical film reformation.
Rapid repassivation after wear-induced film removal determines overall degradation behavior.
The homogenized high-entropy alloy naturally forms a compositionally complex passive oxide film.
Controlled sliding wear in a corrosive electrolyte mechanically disrupts the passive film.
The integrity and composition of the passive oxide film mediate the tribo-corrosion response.
Regions enriched in Cr or other passivating elements support repassivation.
Mechanical wear continuously removes passive film and exposes the underlying metal during tribo-corrosion.
Exposure of the underlying metal triggers formation of a new oxide film.
When repassivation is rapid relative to film removal, total degradation is minimized.
When repassivation is slow relative to film removal, combined degradation is accelerated.
Alloys with faster repassivation kinetics will have lower cumulative degradation than alloys less capable of reforming the protective film.
Faster repassivation will reduce both the wear and corrosion components of degradation.
Increasing wear intensity in an alloy with modest repassivation kinetics will increase total degradation by exposing reactive substrate more frequently.
With minimal mechanical wear, degradation occurs primarily through corrosion without significant mechanical disruption.
The prediction applies when passive-film dynamics are the principal determinant of surface stability, including moderate-temperature and realistic-wear-stress conditions.
The prediction may fail when a very high concentration of passivating elements produces an extremely robust oxide film.
The prediction may fail when extreme pH, high temperature, or aggressive oxidizing conditions independently dominate degradation.
Increasing Cr or another passivating-element content will enhance passive-film stability or repassivation.

contradictions.description: The proposed baseline is not consistent across fields. The intervention and baseline define it as the same or matched alloy under little mechanical wear or a protective overlay, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification experiment define it as a standard or compositionally less-repassivating alloy tested under the same sliding conditions.

The prediction says the faster-repassivating alloy will have lower wear as well as corrosion than the baseline, but the stated baseline experiences minimal mechanical wear. A sliding specimen cannot straightforwardly be predicted to have less wear than a minimal-wear control, so the component-wise comparison is internally inconsistent.
